rv.q: The best thing about Cranston’s turn is that you’re never quite sure when Johnson is being truthful with others — or honest with himself.
But with Cranston commanding the spotlight throughout, All the Way becomes superior entertainment.
Cranston proves so effortlessly captivating that you could imagine pulling a lever for him — or even contributing generously to whatever campaign war chest he trots out.
The TV star’s galvanic turn and the layered, polyphonic production around him take the dried facts of history and make them walk, talk and kick ass to victory.

His many contradictions — egoism battling with insecurity, a natural warmth at odds with a violent temper, a true commitment to the greater good alongside sharklike political instincts — are all given their due, and are expertly synthesized in Mr. Cranston’s terrific portrayal.
Thanks largely to a titanic central performance by Bryan Cranston, it pulls off an astonishing double trick.
Luckily, because Robert Schenkkan’s by-the-numbers historical drama isn’t as compelling as its star.
Through it all, Cranston's LBJ feels a bit like a caricature, but one that's compelling and fun to watch.
The play might be a star vehicle but its star delivers.
It's a brilliant portrayal no less epic than the great tragedies of classic literature.
And, one can argue persuasively, he is using his star power for Good, debuting on Broadway in what is essentially a staged lesson in history and politics.
Still, Schenkkan teases out telling parallels to modern political gridlock, and director Bill Rauch achieves some purely theatrical tableaux.
Cranston is very cranked up as he cajoles, back-pedals, wheedles, whines and lies, and betrays politicians, intimates and even his wife.

And that’s what Cranston delivers big time: a wily, high-strung and very comic LBJ, as if Rip Torn had returned to deliver his measly thug from “Sweet Bird of Youth” with a bit of Walter Brennan thrown in to sweeten the humor.
Schenkkan embraces LBJ's well-documented penchant for raw language, and other traits, without reserve — and Cranston plays them with relish.
It is stalled by countless subplots and lengthy depictions of internal squabbling among the political leaders, many of whom come off as broadly drawn.
If it’s anything like this robust, fascinating look at our recent politics, I can hardly wait to see it.
Onstage, a more modestly designed Bryan Cranston, at maybe 5’10″ and maybe 170 pounds, completely inhabits the bigness of LBJ.
It’s enormous fun to watch Cranston wobbling between arrogance and self-loathing.
